results.message: What did Augustine teach about suicide in the City of God?

voice_event.speaker: lpc
voice_event.text:
Augustine taught on suicide in the City of God, and he began with pity. He wrote of Christian virgins taken captive, some of whom were violated. Some killed themselves to avoid such disgrace. Augustine asked: “So even if some of these virgins killed themselves to escape such disgrace, who with any human feeling would refuse to forgive them? Others would not end their lives, so as not to seem to escape another’s crime by a sin of their own. Whoever charges them with great wickedness for this is himself not free of the fault of folly. It is not lawful to take the law into our own hands and kill even a guilty person, whose death no public sentence has ordered. If so, then surely whoever kills himself commits homicide. He is the guiltier of his own death, the more innocent he was of the offence for which he condemned himself to die.”

Then he gave the hard teaching. He who kills himself is a homicide. The more innocent a man is of the offence he dooms himself for, the guiltier of his own death he is. He named Judas as his example. His words do not say what became of any person who died this way. They say nothing about burial.

names.name: Augustinius of Hippo Regius, presbyter 391, bishop 395/396-430

figures_used.bridge_line: Our bishop at Hippo. The people seized him and brought him to be made a presbyter while he wept. Later they pressed him into the bishop's office over his own refusal. He spent his last days weeping over psalms of penitence, while an army lay outside the walls.

dates.display: converted 386, baptised 387; seized by the congregation at Hippo and ordained presbyter against his own wishes in 391, weeping through it (Possidius, Vita IV); designated coadjutor and consecrated bishop of Hippo by Megalius, primate of Numidia, in 395/396, again amid popular acclamation (Possidius, Vita VIII); died 430, during the Vandal siege of Hippo
